d1.name: Decision Architecture
d1.blurb: Who owns the call, what happens in the 24 hours after it, and whether it stays closed.

d2.name: Signal Intelligence
d2.blurb: Whether the signals reach the people who can act on them, and how early.

d3.name: Organizational Clarity
d3.blurb: Whether your three direct reports would name the same priority, and what a Thursday afternoon looks like.

architect.label: Built For Success
architect.line: Sound architecture that works today. The risk is whether it still works tomorrow.
narrative: Your team knows who decides. When pressure arrives, they move, and the decision holds once it is made. That is rarer than it sounds.

The question your score raises is not whether the architecture works. It is whether it scales. A framework that works at one level of complexity gets stretched at the next, and stretched architecture fails at the worst moment: a regulatory review, a leadership change, a market shift.

One question worth sitting with before the next planning cycle: what happens to your decision process when you are not in the room? If that has a tested answer, you are in strong shape. If it does not, that is the conversation to have before something makes it urgent.

builder.label: First Responder
builder.line: The instincts are right. What is not built yet is the framework that lets your team act on them without you.
narrative: Your instincts are not the problem. Most of the time things get decided, the team moves and results follow. The gap is the structure that makes what you know transferable.
The pattern in organizations that score here: decisions happen when you are in the room. When you are not, they slow down, get revisited or wait. That is a design problem, not a people problem.
Your lowest dimension shows where the gap is widest. That is where the build starts, with a decision framework your team can own and use without you as the reference point.

monitor.label: Spread Too Thin
monitor.line: You are not missing signals. You are reacting to them too late.
narrative: The signals before your last significant problem were there. They almost always are. The question is whether anyone had a clear process for catching them, naming them and bringing them forward before they became pressure.
Right now your organization is responding to waves the ripple announced earlier. That is a watching problem, not a talent problem.

The organizations that close this gap do not buy better dashboards. They build a signal process: a named responsibility, a clear channel and a regular cadence for getting what the front line sees to the people who can act on it. That is buildable, and your team can own it without you managing it daily.

catalyst.label: Constant Firedrill
catalyst.line: The architecture is not weak. It is missing. That is the clearest possible starting point.
narrative: Direct is more useful than encouraging here. Your score says the decision architecture is not weak. It is missing.

Weak architecture produces slow, inconsistent decisions. Missing architecture produces drag that compounds quietly until something breaks: a key client, a regulatory event, a team that stops engaging.

Jack has watched capable organizations reach that point. The ones that came through built the framework before the crisis, not after. That does not take a restructuring or a new initiative. It takes deciding to start now, while there is still room to do it without urgency forcing your hand.

architect_d1.line: Decision Architecture is your lowest score. The calls hold. The question is how much of that is you.
narrative: Decision Architecture came in lowest for you, and at the Built For Success band that is a narrow gap, not a hole. Decisions get made. Owners are named. The team moves and the call stays closed. That is rarer than it sounds.

What the score cannot settle is how much of that holds when you are out of the room. A process that runs on one person's judgment looks the same as a built one, right up to the day that person is on a plane or gone.
The test is simple and rarely run. Step back for two weeks with no email and watch what waits for you. Whatever waits is the part of the architecture that is still you.

architect_d2.line: Signal Intelligence is your lowest score. Your decisions hold. They may be arriving late.
narrative: Signal Intelligence came in lowest for you. At the Built For Success band the decision process is sound. A problem reaches the right people and gets handled. The gap is in how early it reaches them.

A strong process fed late information still produces a late response. The competitor move most of your industry is still reacting to. The person you did not want to lose. The client complaint that became a pattern. Each of those left a trace before it became news.

Ask where your information comes from. If the true answer is your direct reports, you are hearing what has already been filtered. One real conversation three levels down each month changes what you know before the quarter does.

architect_d3.line: Organizational Clarity is your lowest score. The decision holds. The reasons may not travel.
narrative: Organizational Clarity came in lowest for you. At the Built For Success band, decisions get made and stay made. What the score flags is the distance between the call and the people who carry it out.

Here is the test. Name the single most important thing your organization has to do in the next 90 days. Then ask whether your three direct reports would name the same thing. It is easy to assume yes. It is rarer to have checked.

The risk at this band is quiet. A clear decision, delivered once, lands differently on each person who heard it. The follow-up conversations happen without you, and the plan drifts a few degrees before anyone notices. Ask the question this week and listen for the third answer.

builder_d1.line: Decision Architecture is your lowest score. Things get decided when you are in the room.
narrative: Decision Architecture came in lowest for you. At the First Responder band your instincts are good and the results mostly follow. What is not built yet is the structure that makes a decision hold when you are not the one holding it.

The pattern reads like this. A call gets made in the meeting and is back on the table a week later. Approval or more data costs two or three days nobody had. Owners are named in your head and not out loud. None of that is a talent problem. It is a design problem.

Start with one thing: the last decision that would not stay closed. Who owned it, what reopened it, and who decided it was open again? The answers are the first page of the architecture you are missing.

builder_d2.line: Signal Intelligence is your lowest score. You act fast once you know. You find out late.
narrative: Signal Intelligence came in lowest for you. At the First Responder band the response is quick once a problem is on your desk. The gap is the distance between the first sign and your desk, and how much of that trip the signal survives.

Think about the last significant problem: the lost client, the person who left, the missed target. Looking back, the signs were there. They usually are. The question is whether anyone owned the job of catching them and bringing them forward, or whether it depended on who happened to notice.

That is a buildable gap. A named owner, a clear channel and a regular cadence for getting what the front line sees to the person who can act. Until then you are paying for the delay in every problem that grew bigger than it had to.

builder_d3.line: Organizational Clarity is your lowest score. The decision is made. The real vote starts after you leave.
narrative: Organizational Clarity came in lowest for you. At the First Responder band the call gets made and most of the team moves. The gap shows up afterward: clarifying questions, a quiet second debate in the hallway, and a few people who need another conversation before they commit.

That cost is easy to miss because it never shows up as a line item. It shows up as a decision that takes two weeks to become action, as problems sent up to you that your team could have settled, and as a Thursday afternoon where the work gets done and nothing more.

Try one thing before the next planning cycle. Ask your three direct reports, separately, what the top priority is for the next 90 days. If you get three answers, you have found where the build starts.

monitor_d1.line: Decision Architecture is your lowest score. Nobody owns the call, so the call keeps coming back.
narrative: Decision Architecture is where your score is lowest, and at the Spread Too Thin band the gap is not small. Decisions get made and then get made again. Owners are unclear. The meeting gets rescheduled and the miss has no name on it.

What that costs is days, and then quarters. A decision that slips three days in a 48-hour window is a decision that was not made. Over a year that pattern turns into a team that waits to be told and a leader who is more central to daily calls than anyone should be.

A score points at this. It does not prove it. The fix does not start with a new process. It starts with one decision, this week, run differently: a named owner and a date, plus one rule for what it would take to reopen it. Then watch whether it stays closed.

monitor_d2.line: Signal Intelligence is your lowest score. The signals were there. Nobody read them in time.
narrative: Signal Intelligence is where your score is lowest. At the Spread Too Thin band the pattern is not that signals are missed. It is that they are seen late, explained away, or raised only by someone who had to find the nerve to raise them.

The cost is that every problem arrives bigger than it had to be. The client was unhappy for a quarter before the account went. The person who left had been at risk for months. The competitor move surprised you, and most of your energy since has gone to catching up.

Fifteen answers cannot show whether that was one bad year or how things work. You can. If your information reaches you through two layers of direct reports, it has been filtered twice before you see it. Go three levels down this month and ask what people are seeing. Then build the channel so you do not have to.

monitor_d3.line: Organizational Clarity is your lowest score. The team is working hard, and not in the same direction.
narrative: Organizational Clarity is where your score is lowest. At the Spread Too Thin band the pattern is this: you deliver a decision, and the next several days go to winning over people who had not accepted it.

That costs more than time. Problems get sent up to you that your team could have solved, and solving them yourself is faster, so it keeps happening. A missed target creates a cloud that takes weeks to clear. Your most engaged people carry more than their share and are the first to notice.

A quiz cannot settle whether that is the pattern or one bad quarter. One question can. Ask your three direct reports, one at a time, what the single most important thing is for the next 90 days. The answers will tell you how much of your week goes to re-explaining what you thought was settled.

catalyst_d1.line: Decision Architecture is your lowest score. It is not weak. It is missing.
narrative: Decision Architecture is where your score is lowest, and at the Constant Firedrill band the plain reading is that it is not there. When news breaks, the first hours go to working out who should be in the room. When a call is made, it has to be re-explained before anything moves. When you step away, things slow to a crawl.

What that costs is not dramatic on any single day. It is drag. Every decision carries a tax of delay and rework, and the tax builds until something gives: a key client, a regulatory letter, a team that stops raising problems because raising them changes nothing.

A score cannot tell a hard year from the way the place runs. You can. Make one decision this week with a named owner, a date and a written reason, in a way the team could repeat without you. The architecture gets built one decision at a time, and the time to build it is before the next fire.

catalyst_d2.line: Signal Intelligence is your lowest score. You hear about problems when they are already problems.
narrative: Signal Intelligence is where your score is lowest. At the Constant Firedrill band the plain reading is that signals do not reach you. By the time you hear about something, it has already become the thing you are responding to.

The cost shows up as surprise. The competitor move you did not see coming. The person who resigned with no warning you noticed. The regulatory issue that was a murmur for months. Each of those had a first sign somewhere in your organization. The path from that sign to your desk did not exist.

Fifteen answers cannot prove that. One check can. When did you last have a real conversation with someone three or four levels down, outside a town hall or a review? If you cannot remember, that is the first move. Then put a name on the job of catching signals, so it stops depending on who happens to be brave that week.

catalyst_d3.line: Organizational Clarity is your lowest score. The team does not know what you know.
narrative: Organizational Clarity is where your score is lowest. At the Constant Firedrill band the plain reading is that your team is not pulling in one direction, and you may already know it. The energy is managed rather than real. Problems get sent up to you as a matter of course. A miss settles over the place like weather.

That costs you in two places. Every decision you deliver has to be delivered again, so your week goes to re-explaining. And the people doing more than their share can see the ones doing the minimum, which is how you lose the ones you cannot afford to lose.

Start with the question that is easiest to skip. Ask your three direct reports, separately, what the one priority for the next 90 days is. Three different answers is not a verdict. It is the clearest place to begin, because it is a gap you can close in a conversation, and that conversation can happen this week.

headers.3: The one most leaders would rather skip.
headers.4: The test nobody thinks to run.
headers.6: The signals were there. Were you?
headers.7: How far does intelligence travel here?
headers.8: The conversation that doesn't make the report.
headers.9: The move your industry is still reacting to.
headers.10: The person who left. When did you know?
headers.11: Three people. One priority. Do they match?
headers.12: After you leave the room, the real vote begins.
headers.13: The pattern that becomes the culture.

questions.stem: Your organization needed to move fast on a decision. Someone said 'we need approval' or 'we need more data.' What happened next?
opts: We pushed, but the process cost us two or three days we didn't have.
We waited. The moment closed. That pattern repeats more than I'd like to admit.
We moved anyway. We named a deadline and an owner. Approvals and data arrived after.
The meeting got rescheduled. The decision slipped. No one owned the miss.

questions.stem: When a major decision gets made in your organization, what happens in the following 24 hours?
opts: Execution is uneven. Some move. Others wait to be told what they're responsible for.
A plan gets built. Owners are named, roles assigned, and everyone knows who does what.
The decision gets re-explained, restructured, and sometimes remade before anything moves.
Most people execute, but roles and governance get settled in the first few conversations.

questions.stem: Think of the last decision that wouldn't stay closed. Agreed in the meeting, back on the table a week later. What drove that?
opts: There was no clear owner. Everyone felt entitled to weigh back in.
Someone with influence wasn't consulted the first time. Their objection surfaced after the fact.
I'm not sure. Decisions tend to feel unfinished here. That's how it goes.
Genuine new information arrived that changed the picture. We reopened it deliberately.

questions.stem: If you stepped away for two weeks with no access to email or Slack, how would decisions get made?
opts: The team would manage, but with visible hesitation on anything consequential.
Things would slow significantly. I am more central to daily decisions than I should be.
Most things would move. A few decisions would wait for me that probably shouldn't.
The system holds. Named owners, criteria, escalation paths. They decide without me. I've tested it.

questions.stem: News that changes everything landed: a regulatory shift, a competitor move, a market drop. You have 48 hours. What happens in the first four?
opts: We activate a standing response protocol. Roles are clear. We reach a decision within hours.
The first four hours are mostly urgency without direction. We figure it out eventually.
The right people convene quickly. Aligning takes a few hours, but we get there.
We call many meetings. The first few decide who should be in the room.

banner.tag: How well do you see what's coming?

questions.stem: The last serious problem you faced: a lost client, a regulatory issue, a key departure. What was the first sign it was coming?
opts: There were signals. We saw them. We moved too slowly and the problem grew.
In hindsight, obvious. At the time we missed them, or explained them away.
One specific signal, a conversation or data point, caught and acted on before it escalated.
There were signals. Something felt off, but we couldn't read it clearly enough to act.

questions.stem: When someone spots a complaint pattern, a regulatory murmur or a competitor move, how reliably does it reach the people who can act?
opts: Usually. It depends who spots it. Some people raise things, others absorb them quietly.
Reliably. Clear channels, and a shared expectation that signals get raised, wherever they start.
Rarely. By the time we hear it, the signal has usually become a problem.
Inconsistently. Signals reach us when someone has the courage or access to escalate. Many don't.

questions.stem: When did you last talk, outside a town hall, with someone three or four levels below you about where the friction lives?
opts: A few months ago, at least. It's less regular than it should be.
In the last two weeks, deliberately and often. It's how I know what's happening.
I can't remember the last time. My information mostly comes through my direct reports.
In the last month. It happens, though not on a consistent cadence.

questions.stem: Your biggest competitor made a significant move last quarter, one most of your industry is still reacting to. Were you surprised?
opts: Yes. The move caught us off guard. We've been responding since.
No. We had tracked signals pointing to it. We already knew how we'd respond.
I'd rather not answer that in a quiz. But the truthful answer is yes.
Partially. We had some indicators but hadn't connected them. We moved quickly once it happened.

questions.stem: The last person you lost and didn't want to. When did you know they were at risk, and did you act before they resigned?
opts: When they gave notice. In hindsight the signs were there. I wasn't watching closely enough.
When they resigned. I had no indication, or I wasn't paying close enough attention.
I saw it weeks earlier and spoke to them directly. Whatever happened, I had acted.
I sensed something was off. I didn't act in time. Then it was too late.

banner.tag: Does your team know what you know?

questions.stem: The one thing you must accomplish in the next 90 days, without looking it up. Have your three direct reports heard you say it?
opts: Probably. We've talked about priorities recently. But I haven't tested it.
Yes, and I've tested it. I asked them directly, not assumed. We're aligned.
I'm not confident they'd all say the same thing. A gap I've meant to close.
Maybe two of the three. I suspect the third would say something different.

questions.stem: The last time you delivered a major decision or direction change to your team. After that conversation ended, what happened next?
opts: A follow-up was needed. Some were on board, others privately uncertain and needing time.
The real debate started afterward. Days went to re-aligning people who hadn't accepted the decision.
The team moved to execution. The why and the what were clear. No follow-up needed.
Clarifying questions came in the next day or two, but momentum moved toward execution.

questions.stem: What's typical in your organization when someone escalates a problem to leadership that they could have solved themselves?
opts: We solve it. It's faster. It happens so often nobody flags it as a pattern.
We redirect it. People know the difference between what needs leadership and what doesn't.
Escalation is how things get done. Leadership solves problems from below. It's the culture now.
We help, but we name it. The boundary is understood, even if sometimes crossed.

questions.stem: Your team on a regular Thursday afternoon. No sprint, no deadline, no crisis. What are people doing?
opts: Taking initiative on things nobody assigned. They own outcomes. It shows when nobody is watching.
Going through the motions. The energy is managed, not real. I can feel the difference.
Getting the work done reliably. The commitment is real but task-driven. Initiative appears when directed.
Completing what's required. The engaged carry more than their share. The rest do the minimum.

questions.stem: Your organization just missed a target. Not catastrophically, but meaningfully. Walk me through the next 72 hours.
opts: People get cautious. The miss creates more instability than it warranted, and recovery is slow.
The debrief takes a few days. Confidence dips, then recovers. The response comes together, slowly.
A miss leaves a cloud that lingers. Some get stuck in it. The cost compounds.
Within 48 hours: named cause, named owner, revised plan. No blame. We move.
